implementation_notes: Kotlin persists through the same Jakarta Persistence/Hibernate strategy as Java: annotate the abstract base with @Inheritance(strategy = InheritanceType.TABLE_PER_CLASS) and each concrete class gets its own table with the inherited columns repeated, with polymorphic queries executed as a union. Two Kotlin specifics matter: entity classes are final and have no no-arg constructor by default, so the kotlin-jpa plugin (no-arg plus all-open) is required for Hibernate to instantiate and proxy them; and IDENTITY generation is unusable because each table would mint its own keys. The classic structure is still justified when the hierarchy is stable and reads are leaf-scoped.
pitfalls: Entity classes are final and lack a no-arg constructor: without the kotlin-jpa (no-arg/all-open) plugin Hibernate cannot instantiate them and lazy proxies fail.
IDENTITY generation is not usable with TABLE_PER_CLASS - use a shared sequence, table generator or UUID, or keys collide across the hierarchy.
TABLE_PER_CLASS support is optional in Jakarta Persistence and provider-specific, so a portable Kotlin codebase cannot depend on it.

variants.name: Exposed with one Table object per concrete class
variants.idiom_name: Exposed Table object + row class per concrete type, unionAll for mixed reads
variants.implementation_notes: JetBrains' Exposed has no inheritance mapping at all: a table is an object extending Table and a row is an ordinary data class, so one Table object plus one row class per concrete type is already the pattern, with the shared columns repeated in each definition. Mixed collections need unionAll over queries with matching column lists, or one query per type merged in Kotlin. Choose this when you want a Kotlin-first DSL and explicit SQL without JPA's entity lifecycle; the JPA route remains the alternative when the team already runs a Jakarta Persistence stack.
pitfalls: Exposed generates its own auto-increment/serial ids per table, so keys are not unique across the hierarchy - use a UUID column or a shared key table.
unionAll demands identical column lists on both sides, so the shared columns must be projected explicitly (and missing ones padded) for every mixed read.
A change to a shared column must be edited in every Table object and every migration; nothing links the definitions.
